summary.text: Taking $p=7$ and $r=6$, a finite recurrence evaluation of the binomial sums gives $a(7^6)-a(7^5)\equiv 6\cdot 7^{24}\pmod{7^{25}}$. Since this residue is nonzero modulo $7^{25}$, these parameters provide a counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom nk^2\binom{n+k-1}{k}^2.
\]
We give a counterexample with
\[
p=7,\qquad r=6.
\]
The two arguments of the sequence that occur in the proposed congruence are then
\[
p^r=7^6=117649,
\qquad
p^{r-1}=7^5=16807,
\]
and the proposed modulus is
\[
p^{4r+1}=7^{4\cdot6+1}=7^{25}.
\]
We will calculate both sums modulo this modulus and show that their difference is divisible by \(7^{24}\), but not by \(7^{25}\).

Set
\[
M=7^{25}=1341068619663964900807.
\]
The following recurrence gives a convenient exact finite calculation of the sums. For a fixed positive integer \(n\), put
\[
B_k=\binom nk,
\qquad
C_k=\binom{n+k-1}{k}.
\]
At \(k=0\), both values are \(1\). The standard consecutive-binomial identities give
\[
B_{k+1}=B_k\frac{n-k}{k+1}
\tag{1}
\]
and
\[
C_{k+1}=C_k\frac{n+k}{k+1}.
\tag{2}
\]
Indeed,
\[
\binom n{k+1}=\binom nk\frac{n-k}{k+1},
\]
while
\[
\binom{n+k}{k+1}
 =\binom{n+k-1}{k}\frac{n+k}{k+1}.
\]
Thus, starting with \(B_0=C_0=1\), equations (1) and (2) produce exactly the two binomial coefficients needed in each summand. After adding \(B_k^2C_k^2\) for \(k=0,1,\ldots,n-1\), the accumulator is exactly \(a(n)\).

For completeness, we now describe how this recurrence was evaluated modulo \(M\) without ever making an invalid division modulo a power of \(7\). For every positive integer \(x\), write
\[
x=7^{v_7(x)}x^*,
\qquad 7\nmid x^*.
\]
At each stage represent the binomial coefficients as
\[
B_k=7^{b_k}U_k,
\qquad
C_k=7^{c_k}V_k,
\]
where \(b_k=v_7(B_k)\), \(c_k=v_7(C_k)\), and retain the unit factors \(U_k,V_k\) modulo \(M\). Initially
\[
b_0=c_0=0,
\qquad
U_0=V_0=1.
\]
Stripping the powers of \(7\) from the numerator and denominator in (1) gives the updates
\[
b_{k+1}
 =b_k+v_7(n-k)-v_7(k+1),
\tag{3}
\]
\[
U_{k+1}
 \equiv U_k (n-k)^*\bigl((k+1)^*\bigr)^{-1}\pmod M.
\tag{4}
\]
Likewise, equation (2) gives
\[
c_{k+1}
 =c_k+v_7(n+k)-v_7(k+1),
\tag{5}
\]
\[
V_{k+1}
 \equiv V_k (n+k)^*\bigl((k+1)^*\bigr)^{-1}\pmod M.
\tag{6}
\]
The inverses in (4) and (6) exist because the starred quantities are not divisible by \(7\), and hence are relatively prime to \(M=7^{25}\). Equations (1) and (2) show inductively that (3)--(6) retain precisely the valuations and unit parts of the actual integer binomial coefficients.

The \(k\)-th summand has valuation
\[
w_k=v_7(B_k^2C_k^2)=2(b_k+c_k).
\]
There are two cases in the modular accumulation. If \(w_k\geq25\), then the summand is \(0\pmod M\). If \(w_k<25\), its residue is
\[
7^{w_k}U_k^2V_k^2\pmod M.
\tag{7}
\]
Consequently, (3)--(7), together with the initial state above, completely specify a finite calculation of \(a(n)\pmod M\) using only integer valuations, multiplication, addition, and inversion of numbers coprime to \(7\).

Here is the valuation count produced during the calculation. The entry in column \(w\) is the number of summands for which \(w_k=w\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr}
 n & w=0&w=4&w=8&w=12&w=16&w=20&w=24\\ \hline
16807  &1&6&42&294&2058&14406&0\\
117649 &1&6&42&294&2058&14406&100842
\end{array}
\]
The first row counts
\[
1+6+42+294+2058+14406=16807
\]
summands, and the second counts
\[
1+6+42+294+2058+14406+100842=117649
\]
summands, so every term in each defining sum is included. In particular, in these two calculations every summand has valuation at most \(24\), and formula (7) handles all of them.

To display the modular additions compactly, write residues as 25-digit base-\(7\) strings, padding on the left with zeroes. The following table gives the accumulator after the first \(K\) summands, i.e. after summing over \(0\leq k<K\). Each row follows from repeatedly applying (3)--(7):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
 n&K&\text{partial sum modulo }7^{25}\text{, in base }7\\ \hline
16807&1&0000000000000000000000001\\
16807&7&4252000000000000000000001\\
16807&49&2606425200000000000000001\\
16807&343&0256666642520000000000001\\
16807&2401&3412555126403252000000001\\
16807&16807&5200321453513624634200001\\ \hline
117649&1&0000000000000000000000001\\
117649&7&0000000000000000000000001\\
117649&49&4252000000000000000000001\\
117649&343&2606425200000000000000001\\
117649&2401&0256666642520000000000001\\
117649&16807&3412555126403252000000001\\
117649&117649&4200321453513624634200001
\end{array}
\]
The last entry in each block is the corresponding complete defining sum. Therefore
\[
a(16807)\equiv (5200321453513624634200001)_7\pmod{7^{25}},
\tag{8}
\]
and
\[
a(117649)\equiv (4200321453513624634200001)_7\pmod{7^{25}}.
\tag{9}
\]
In decimal form, these residues are respectively
\[
a(16807)\equiv1012908569057404849376\pmod M
\]
and
\[
a(117649)\equiv821327337676838434975\pmod M.
\]
The lower 24 base-\(7\) digits in (8) and (9) are identical, while the leading digit changes from \(5\) to \(4\). Hence their difference is
\[
a(117649)-a(16807)
 \equiv -7^{24}
 \equiv 6\cdot7^{24}
 \pmod{7^{25}}.
\tag{10}
\]
Numerically,
\[
7^{24}=191581231380566414401,
\]
and indeed the displayed least nonnegative residues differ by exactly its negative. The residue \(6\cdot7^{24}\) in (10) is not zero modulo \(7^{25}\), because \(7\nmid6\). Thus
\[
a(117649)\not\equiv a(16807)\pmod{7^{25}}.
\]

Finally, \(7\) is prime, \(7\geq7\), and \(r=6\geq2\). Therefore \((p,r)=(7,6)\) satisfies every hypothesis of the conjecture, but its asserted congruence would be
\[
a(7^6)\equiv a(7^5)\pmod{7^{4\cdot6+1}},
\]
which is exactly the false congruence ruled out above. This counterexample disproves the universal conjecture.
